summary: Describes two TFTP options: one to negotiate the retransmission timeout interval, and one to tell the receiver the transfer size before it begins. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two extra agreements for file swapping: how long to wait before asking again, and how big the file is up front.

subtitle: Two TFTP options: agree on the retransmission timeout, and learn the file size before the transfer starts.

tldr.problem: Basic TFTP gives the two sides no way to agree on how long to wait before retransmitting, and the receiver cannot know the size of the file up front.
tldr.mechanism: The request carries a timeout option holding seconds (1 to 255), or a tsize option holding the file size in octets. The server confirms with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK).
tldr.outcome: A receiver can check that a file fits before accepting it and abort with error code 3 if it is too large, and both sides can use a timeout they agreed on.

facts.label: Size in read requests
facts.value: 0 in the request, real size in the OACK

today: RFC 2349 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1784 and updates RFC 1350. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Small Extensions
sections.content:
TFTP is a simple, lock-step protocol that lets a client get or put a file on a remote host. This RFC describes two options for it. The first lets the client and server negotiate the timeout interval. The second lets the side receiving the file learn the final size of the transfer before it begins.

Both use the TFTP option extension mechanism of RFC 2347: extra NULL-terminated name and value fields appended to the read request or write request.
sections.plainLanguage: Two little notes you can add to a file request: "wait this long before nagging me" and "the file is this big."

sections.title: The Timeout Interval Option
sections.content:
After the mode, the request carries the option name timeout (case-insensitive) and a number of seconds in ASCII. Valid values are 1 to 255, inclusive. The number says how long to wait before retransmitting.

If the server accepts, it replies with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK), and the timeout value in it must match the value the client sent. The RFC's example is a read request for foobar in octet mode with a timeout of 1 second.
sections.plainLanguage: You say how long you will wait before asking again, and the other side has to agree to exactly that number.

sections.title: The Transfer Size Option
sections.content:
The request carries tsize (case-insensitive) and a size in ASCII. In a read request the client sends a size of 0, and the server returns the real file size in octets in its OACK. In a write request the client states the file size in octets, and the server echoes it back in the OACK.

If the file is too large for the receiving side to handle, that side may abort the transfer with an ERROR packet using error code 3. The RFC's example is a write request for the 673312-octet file foobar.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the boxes arrive, you learn how many there will be. If your room is too small, you can say no right away.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The basic TFTP protocol has no security mechanism, which is why it has no rename, delete or file overwrite capabilities. This document adds no security to TFTP. The RFC states that the specified extensions do not add any additional security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP never had locks on its doors, and these notes do not add any, but they do not open any new doors either.

messages.label: Read Request, tsize = 0
messages.note: The client asks for the file and sends a size of 0.

messages.label: OACK, tsize = file size
messages.note: The server returns the file size in octets.

messages.label: ERROR code 3 (optional)
messages.note: The client may abort if the file is too large for it.
